analysis.one_liner: Sets a national floor for how companies collect, share, and secure Americans' personal data, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 25, 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create the first general federal consumer privacy law. Companies that collect personal data would need notice-and-consent, with express opt-in consent for sensitive data like health records, biometrics, and precise location. People would gain rights to see, correct, and delete their data, and companies would have to run a written data security program, with enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general carrying civil penalties of up to $42,530 per affected person. At the same time, it would override state privacy laws the moment it is enacted, even though its own protections would not take effect for a year, and it gives individuals no right to sue violators themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Every internet-connected consumer. The bill grants rights to access, correct, and delete personal data a company holds; requires clear privacy policies; forces express consent before a company collects sensitive data (health, biometrics, precise location, religion, race, sexual orientation); requires a documented data security program; and lets the FTC and state attorneys general impose penalties scaled to the number of people affected [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Companies may collect sensitive personal data — health, biometric, precise location, religion, race, sexual orientation — only with express affirmative consent that cannot be inferred from inaction [S2].

Individuals get a right to access and export their data, correct inaccuracies, and have data deleted, at no charge for at least two requests per year, and companies must provide easy-to-use controls for free [S2].

Every covered entity and service provider must maintain a comprehensive data security program, with safeguards scaled to the sensitivity of the data and the risk of identity theft or physical injury [S2].
Enforcement carries real teeth: civil penalties of up to $42,530 per individual affected, enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general on behalf of residents [S2].

The FTC would hire at least 440 additional enforcement personnel, and covered entities handling data on more than 20 million people must designate a privacy officer and run documented privacy impact assessments [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and process personal data — large platforms, data brokers, and their service providers — bear new compliance costs: consent systems, privacy policies, security programs, and for large firms, privacy officers and impact assessments. Consumers also pay a cost the bill does not advertise: the moment it is enacted it wipes out state privacy laws, including stronger state regimes, before the federal protections even begin, and people cannot sue violators directly [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Data companies — and consumers losing state protections

drawbacks.text: State preemption takes effect immediately upon enactment, while the bill's substantive protections do not take effect until one year after enactment [S2]. In the gap, and permanently thereafter, stronger state privacy laws are superseded [S2].

For non-sensitive data, the bill defaults to implicit consent: an individual is deemed to have consented if they simply fail to decline a request after notice — an opt-out regime rather than the opt-in regime most privacy advocates favor [S2].
There is no private right of action: only the FTC and state attorneys general may enforce the law, so an individual harmed by a violation cannot sue [S2].

Exemptions narrow the coverage: employee data, publicly available information, and de-identified or pseudonymized data are excluded from the definition of personal data, and small businesses are exempt from the access and correction rights entirely [S2].

Enforcement actions brought by the FTC block state attorneys general from acting against the same defendant on the same facts while the federal case is pending, potentially slowing state-level enforcement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give Americans a uniform set of privacy rights and security requirements they currently lack under federal law, with meaningful penalties and express consent for the most sensitive data. But its design trades strength for industry acceptability: opt-out consent for ordinary data, no right to sue, carve-outs for employers and small businesses, and — most significantly — immediate preemption of state laws before federal protections begin. Whether that trade is worth it depends on whether the FTC and state attorneys general enforce it aggressively; individuals themselves are given no direct remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Commerce Committee, and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran introduced S. 4211 on March 25, 2026, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S4].
No other action has been taken; the bill has zero cosponsors [S3][S4].
A single referred bill with no cosponsors and no committee activity this early in a Congress is not dead, but it has not generated the support needed to move [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote taken, nothing has changed: data companies continue operating under the current patchwork with no new federal obligations, and consumers keep whatever state privacy laws already apply to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: data companies and consumers alike

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it is his bill and he is currently its only supporter on the record.

sides.party_line_note: No one besides the sponsor has taken a position on the record — zero cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.note: These firms profit from assembling and selling profiles of individuals, and the bill's implicit-consent default lets them keep collecting ordinary data unless a person opts out — while preemption shields them from stronger state laws. But they would face new duties for the first time, including express consent for sensitive data, deletion rights, and per-person civil penalties.

Platforms would shoulder the heaviest compliance burden: privacy officers, impact assessments, consent systems, and penalties up to $42,530 per affected person, because they process data on far more than 20 million people. The opt-out consent model and immediate preemption of stricter state regimes would also spare them more aggressive regulation.

industries.industry: Small businesses (under 500 employees, under $50M receipts, under 1M individuals' data)
industries.note: Small businesses are exempt from the access and correction rights and get leniency timelines on deletion requests, sparing them compliance costs. Consumers lose some rights when dealing with them.

industries.industry: Privacy compliance and security software providers
industries.note: Every covered entity must build a documented security program, consent mechanisms, and privacy policies, creating demand for compliance tools and audits.

Employee data is carved out of the definition of personal data entirely, and state employment-data laws are preserved, so workplace surveillance data gets no new protection — a gain for employers who monitor workers.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee movement, this bill is on the standard path for a referred Senate bill: likely to sit in the Commerce Committee unless it picks up bipartisan support or gets attached to a larger package. A first-time federal privacy framework this sweeping has never cleared Congress without sustained cross-party leadership, so the realistic outlook is no further action before this Congress ends.
